Title: Using Threads to Run Code Simultaneously - The Rust Programming Language
URL: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/ch16-01-threads.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Splitting the computation in your program into multiple threads to run multiple tasks at the same time can improve performance, but it also adds complexity. Because threads can run simultaneously, there’s no inherent guarantee about the order in which parts of your code on different threads will run. This can lead to problems, such as:

- Race conditions, in which threads are accessing data or resources in an inconsistent order
- Deadlocks, in which two threads are waiting for each other, preventing both threads from continuing
- Bugs that only happen in certain situations and are hard to reproduce and fix reliably

...

Programming languages implement threads in a few different ways, and many operating systems provide an API the programming language can call for creating new threads. The Rust standard library uses a 1:1 model of thread implementation, whereby a program uses one operating system thread per one language thread. There are crates that implement other models of threading that make different trade-offs to the 1:1 model. (Rust’s async system, which we will see in the next chapter, provides another approach to concurrency as well.)

...

To create a new thread, we call the `thread::spawn` function and pass it a closure (we talked about closures in Chapter 13) containing the code we want to run in the new thread. The example in Listing 16-1 prints some text from a main thread and other text from a new thread.

Filename: src/main.rs

```rust
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    thread::spawn(|| {
        for i in 1..10 {
            println!("hi number {i} from the spawned thread!");
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
        }
    });

    for i in 1..5 {
        println!("hi number {i} from the main thread!");
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
    }
}
```

...

Note that when the main thread of a Rust program completes, all spawned threads are shut down, whether or not they have finished running. The output from this program might be a little different every time, but it will look similar to the following:

```text
hi number 1 from the main thread!
hi number 1 from the spawned thread!
hi number 2 from the main thread!
hi number 2 from the spawned thread!
hi number 3 from the main thread!
hi number 3 from the spawned thread!
hi number 4 from the main thread!
hi number 4 from the spawned thread!
hi number 5 from the spawned thread!

```

The calls to `thread::sleep` force a thread to stop its execution for a short duration, allowing a different thread to run. The threads will probably take turns, but that isn’t guaranteed: It depends on how your operating system schedules the threads. In this run, the main thread printed first, even though the print statement from the spawned thread appears first in the code. And even though we told the spawned thread to print until `i` is `9`, it only got to `5` before the main thread shut down.

...

If you run this code and only see output from the main thread, or don’t see any overlap, ... increasing the ... the ... to create ... for the ... to switch between the threads.

...

The code in Listing 16-1 not only stops the spawned thread prematurely most of the time due to the main thread ending, but because there is no guarantee on the order in which threads run, we also can’t guarantee that the spawned thread will get to run at all!

...

We can fix the problem of the spawned thread not running or of it ending prematurely by saving the return value of `thread::spawn` in a variable. The return type of `thread::spawn` is `JoinHandle `. A `JoinHandle ` is an owned value that, when we call the `join` method on it, will wait for its thread to finish. Listing 16-2 shows how to use the `JoinHandle ` of the thread we created in Listing 16-1 and how to call `join` to make sure the spawned thread finishes before `main` exits.

```
pub fn sleep(dur: Duration)
```

Expand description

Puts the current thread to sleep for at least the specified amount of time.

The thread may sleep longer than the duration specified due to scheduling specifics or platform-dependent functionality. It will never sleep less.

This function is blocking, and should not be used in `async` functions.

## § Platform-specific behavior

On Unix platforms, the underlying syscall may be interrupted by a spurious wakeup or signal handler. To ensure the sleep occurs for at least the specified duration, this function may invoke that system call multiple times. Platforms which do not support nanosecond precision for sleeping will have `dur` rounded up to the nearest granularity of time they can sleep for.

Currently, specifying a zero duration on Unix platforms returns immediately without invoking the underlying `nanosleep` syscall, whereas on Windows platforms the underlying `Sleep` syscall is always invoked. If the intention is to yield the current time-slice you may want to use `yield_now` instead.

...

## § Examples

```
use std::{thread, time};

let ten_millis = time::Duration::from_millis(10);
let now = time::Instant::now();

thread::sleep(ten_millis);

assert!(now.elapsed() >= ten_millis);
```

Every thread is equipped with some basic low-level blocking support, via the `thread::park` function and `thread::Thread::unpark` method. `park` blocks the current thread, which can then be resumed from another thread by calling the `unpark` method on the blocked thread’s handle.

Conceptually, each `Thread` handle has an associated token, which is initially not present:

- The `thread::park` function blocks the current thread unless or until the token is available for its thread handle, at which point it atomically consumes the token. It may also return spuriously, without consuming the token. `thread::park_timeout` does the same, but allows specifying a maximum time to block the thread for.
- The `unpark` method on a `Thread` atomically makes the token available if it wasn’t already. Because the token can be held by a thread even if it is currently not parked, `unpark` followed by `park` will result in the second call returning immediately. However, note that to rely on this guarantee, you need to make sure that your `unpark` happens after all `park` that may be done by other data structures!

Ownership is a set of rules that govern how a Rust program manages memory. All programs have to manage the way they use a computer’s memory while running. Some languages have garbage collection that regularly looks for no-longer-used memory as the program runs; in other languages, the programmer must explicitly allocate and free the memory. Rust uses a third approach: Memory is managed through a system of ownership with a set of rules that the compiler checks. If any of the rules are violated, the program won’t compile. None of the features of ownership will slow down your program while it’s running.

That first part is done by us: When we call `String::from`, its implementation requests the memory it needs. This is pretty much universal in programming languages.

However, the second part is different. In languages with a garbage collector (GC), the GC keeps track of and cleans up memory that isn’t being used anymore, and we don’t need to think about it. In most languages without a GC, it’s our responsibility to identify when memory is no longer being used and to call code to explicitly free it, just as we did to request it. Doing this correctly has historically been a difficult programming problem. If we forget, we’ll waste memory. If we do it too early, we’ll have an invalid variable. If we do it twice, that’s a bug too. We need to pair exactly one `allocate` with exactly one `free`.

Rust takes a different path: The memory is automatically returned once the variable that owns it goes out of scope. Here’s a version of our scope example from Listing 4-1 using a `String` instead of a string literal:

```rust
fn main() {
    {
        let s = String::from("hello"); // s is valid from this point forward

        // do stuff with s
    }                                  // this scope is now over, and s is no
                                       // longer valid
}
```

...

There is a natural point at which we can return the memory our `String` needs to the allocator: when `s` goes out of scope. When a variable goes out of scope, Rust calls a special function for us. This function is called `drop`, and it’s where the author of `String` can put the code to return the memory. Rust calls `drop` automatically at the closing curly bracket.

Title: Using Threads to Run Code Simultaneously - The Rust Programming Language
URL: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/ch16-01-threads.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Splitting the computation in your program into multiple threads to run multiple tasks at the same time can improve performance, but it also adds complexity. Because threads can run simultaneously, there’s no inherent guarantee about the order in which parts of your code on different threads will run. This can lead to problems, such as:

- Race conditions, in which threads are accessing data or resources in an inconsistent order
- Deadlocks, in which two threads are waiting for each other, preventing both threads from continuing
- Bugs that only happen in certain situations and are hard to reproduce and fix reliably

...

Programming languages implement threads in a few different ways, and many operating systems provide an API the programming language can call for creating new threads. The Rust standard library uses a 1:1 model of thread implementation, whereby a program uses one operating system thread per one language thread. There are crates that implement other models of threading that make different trade-offs to the 1:1 model. (Rust’s async system, which we will see in the next chapter, provides another approach to concurrency as well.)

...

To create a new thread, we call the `thread::spawn` function and pass it a closure (we talked about closures in Chapter 13) containing the code we want to run in the new thread. The example in Listing 16-1 prints some text from a main thread and other text from a new thread.

Filename: src/main.rs

```rust
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    thread::spawn(|| {
        for i in 1..10 {
            println!("hi number {i} from the spawned thread!");
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
        }
    });

    for i in 1..5 {
        println!("hi number {i} from the main thread!");
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
    }
}
```

...

Note that when the main thread of a Rust program completes, all spawned threads are shut down, whether or not they have finished running. The output from this program might be a little different every time, but it will look similar to the following:

```text
hi number 1 from the main thread!
hi number 1 from the spawned thread!
hi number 2 from the main thread!
hi number 2 from the spawned thread!
hi number 3 from the main thread!
hi number 3 from the spawned thread!
hi number 4 from the main thread!
hi number 4 from the spawned thread!
hi number 5 from the spawned thread!

```

The calls to `thread::sleep` force a thread to stop its execution for a short duration, allowing a different thread to run. The threads will probably take turns, but that isn’t guaranteed: It depends on how your operating system schedules the threads. In this run, the main thread printed first, even though the print statement from the spawned thread appears first in the code. And even though we told the spawned thread to print until `i` is `9`, it only got to `5` before the main thread shut down.

The code in Listing 16-1 not only stops the spawned thread prematurely most of the time due to the main thread ending, but because there is no guarantee on the order in which threads run, we also can’t guarantee that the spawned thread will get to run at all!

...

We can fix the problem of the spawned thread not running or of it ending prematurely by saving the return value of `thread::spawn` in a variable. The return type of `thread::spawn` is `JoinHandle `. A `JoinHandle ` is an owned value that, when we call the `join` method on it, will wait for its thread to finish.     def _reject(self, race: _Race, record: dict[str, Any], reason: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
        rejected = {**record, "applied": False, "reason": reason, "rejected_ns": time.monotonic_ns()}
        race.rejected_commands.append(rejected)
        return {**rejected, "observation": self.observe(race.race_id)}

    @staticmethod
    def _end(race: _Race, reason: str) -> None:
        race.status = "completed" if reason == "completed" else "failed" if reason == "deadline" or reason.startswith("runtime_error") else "stopped"
        race.reason = reason
        race.finished_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
        race.diagnostics.stop()
        if race.sleeper is not None:
            race.sleeper.close()
        if race.pending is not None:
            _, future = race.pending
            race.pending = None
            if not future.done():
                future.set_exception(ValueError(f"Race ended before input application: {reason}"))

    def _timing(self, race: _Race, diagnostics_detail: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]:
        now_ns = race.finished_ns or time.monotonic_ns()
        wall_elapsed = (now_ns - race.started_ns) / 1e9
        drift_ms = (wall_elapsed - race.sim.elapsed) * 1000
        maximum = max(race.lateness_ms, default=0.0)
        p95 = _percentile(race.lateness_ms, 0.95)
        return {
            "wall_elapsed": wall_elapsed, "simulation_elapsed": race.sim.elapsed,
            "drift_ms": drift_ms, "max_lateness_ms": maximum, "p95_lateness_ms": p95,
            "physics_hz": round(1 / DT), "physics_steps": race.sim.tick,
            "clock_mode": NATIVE_CLOCK_MODE if race.sleeper is not None else ASYNCIO_CLOCK_MODE,
            "pacing": {"native_sleeper_ready_ns": race.sleeper.ready_ns if race.sleeper else None,
                       "native_sleeper_thread_alive": race.sleeper.thread.is_alive() if race.sleeper else False},
            "diagnostics": race.diagnostics.snapshot(detail=diagnostics_detail),
            # A delayed run remains playable but cannot establish viability.
            "infrastructure_valid": maximum <= 100 and p95 <= 25 and abs(drift_ms) <= 100 and not (race.reason or "").startswith("runtime_error"),
            "validity_limits_ms": {"max_lateness": 100, "p95_lateness": 25, "absolute_drift": 100},
        }

# MCP Kart revival plan

Updated October 18, 2026. The first experiment and three telemetry iterations are implemented; screens have not established realtime driving viability. The [compact navigation iteration](experiments/0003-jev-navigation.md) tested observations, control wording and strategy instructions. The subsequent [gate/history experiment](experiments/0004-gates-and-observation-history.md) added explicit checkpoint geometry and past-only motion history; its new model screens were timing-invalid, and free controls reproduced local clock delays. The requested [process isolation](experiments/0005-isolated-physics-clock.md) passes three initial scripted controls, including an HTTP-process pause, with the existing limits. A Jev screen had valid timing but reached only 63/120 gates. Later independent-clock diagnostics and a native sleeper control still failed timing, so reliability remains unresolved and paid testing is held. The native pacer remains an explicit diagnostic option; process-isolated asyncio pacing is the default. Road-physics remains the default observation candidate; no three-lap model completion has been established.

The first question is whether decision models can drive a kart in real time through MCP. The user narrowed the initial PoC to TypeSafe Jev 1.14 through OpenRouter on October 18. OpenAI Decisions and Cloudflare Clef remain later validation targets; existing measurements are preserved. The eventual product is a fun way for developers to experience the trade-off between model speed and intelligence by watching autonomous kart races.

The [Linux Docker comparison](experiments/0006-linux-docker-clock.md) also failed
its first timing control (104.26 ms maximum), despite completing all three laps.
It recorded a 102 ms state-publication span with substantial process CPU, a
different diagnostic from the low-CPU Mac bursts. Docker/container support is
implemented, but the reliability gate still holds Jev; the next investigation
is staged/thread-specific profiling around state publication.

## Confirmed first milestone

- A solo kart completes three laps of a winding track at a useful racing speed.
- The initial target was eight completed runs out of ten without resets, and median completed race time within twice the scripted reference. During implementation the user added off-track rescue; the assisted experiment retains the completion/pace target but reports rescue counts and zero-rescue completions separately. Freeze track and vehicle handling within each comparison.
- The driver chooses steering, throttle, and braking directly. There is no automatic lane keeping or racing-line follower.
- Physics advances continuously in wall-clock time while model requests are in flight. The kart holds its last control input between decisions.
- Faster models get more opportunities to act: keep one request in flight per kart, apply its reply, then collect the next observation without imposing a common decision cadence.
- A thin Python driver converts Decisions choices into MCP control calls. Access models through OpenRouter's Decisions endpoint. Codex, Claude Code, and other general-purpose agent clients are evaluated later.
- The model receives structured telemetry and upcoming track geometry, including position, heading, velocity, and road boundaries, without suggested steering inputs. Image-based driving is a later experiment.
- A scripted driver establishes that the same track and physics are driveable and provides a comparison for the model.
- Start the simulation in Python as well. Consider Rust only if measured simulation or scheduling costs interfere with realtime operation.
- Development is local, with a 2D SVG spectator view. Traffic, collisions, and power-ups follow the solo milestone.
- Going off-road slows the kart down. After three continuous seconds off-road, a configurable rescue returns it near its departure point, aligned with the road, stopped and coasting. The clock and checkpoint progress continue; the teleport grants no progress. Older model replies are discarded after rescue. Ordered checkpoints prevent skipped gates, but permit ordinary corner clipping between gates.
- The first paid experiment batch has a total spending cap of $10 across all models.
- Current testing focuses on Jev. Establish passing solo driving before resuming other models; a Jev pass does not establish their performance.

These decisions were confirmed through the interview and the switch to OpenRouter. [The realtime timing decision](adr/0001-racing-time-is-independent-of-model-responses.md) preserves the intended comparison between intelligence and latency. The [first experiment specification](experiments/0001-realtime-driving.md) turns this scope into a reviewable implementation plan.

## What the first milestone establishes

A successful result establishes solo driving with this model, driver, observation format, track, and local network conditions. Competitive racing, general-purpose agent clients, multiplayer capacity, and production latency each require additional experiments.

## Experiment sequence

The following sequence implements the approved first experiment.

1. **Endpoint smoke test.** Confirm access to OpenRouter's `POST /api/alpha/decisions` with the three requested models. Record the request shape, model, provider, and failure modes without logging credentials.
2. **Physics reference.** Establish continuous simulation, a winding track, and a scripted driver. Measure simulation scheduling separately from inference. Freeze track difficulty and handling before measuring the model.
3. **Delay tolerance.** Inject controlled observation and action delays into the scripted driver. Determine which delays and jitter prevent it from maintaining control. This diagnoses sensitivity; it does not establish that a model will drive equally well.
4. **Decision latency.** Measure realistic changing observations and a small fixed control menu using a reused connection. Pin exact models and providers, disable automatic fallbacks and hidden retries, and record the actual returned route. Report sample counts, warm and cold behavior, latency distributions, errors, rate limits, and input usage.
5. **Closed-loop driving.** Run the Decisions driver through MCP while physics keeps advancing. Capture the observation, chosen action, when that action took effect, and a spectator replay. Compare completion and driving performance with the reference.
6. **Failure diagnosis.** Compare the same driver with and without MCP overhead, different action grids, and different observation sizes. Keep direct transport runs separate from the MCP milestone. Distinguish latency failures from poor decisions, incomplete observations, or inadequate controls.

The critical timing measure is **observation age when the action takes effect**, not time to first token. Capture observation time, request start, complete response, and action application using one monotonic clock wherever possible. Also measure simulation lateness so an overloaded Python loop cannot silently slow the game.

Track completion, progress, off-track time, lap times, action age, rejected or late actions, errors, and cost. Include sample counts with percentiles; a small smoke test cannot characterize the latency tail.

## Decisions API findings

OpenRouter documents a shared [Decisions endpoint](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/alphadecisions/submit-a-decisions-request) for the requested models. It accepts structured state and named questions, and returns choices or scores rather than requesting tool calls. The initial comparison uses `typesafe/jev-1.14`, `cloudflare/clef`, and `openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions`; Clef Flash is a possible additional comparison.

The driver asks for one choice among 15 explicit low-level control combinations and maps the answer to an MCP call. A joint choice keeps steering and acceleration decisions coupled. A score is a probability-weighted rubric result, not a generated steering angle.

The user supplied an OpenRouter API key locally as `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, and initial measurements are underway; ChatGPT/Codex login is not part of the experiment's authentication. [The API research notes](research/decision-models.md) record the verified endpoints, schemas, model identities, and routing considerations.

## Temporal and language boundary

Proposed: keep the first physics and inference timing loop independent of Temporal, then add Temporal orchestration and measure its effect. The first simulation will use Python; benchmark simulation scheduling before deciding whether Rust is needed.

For the platform, a Race Workflow could own admission, start, cancellation, completion, and results while a separate runtime executes continuous physics. A long-running Activity and an external race service are both candidates; recovery and interruption semantics need an explicit design.

[Temporal's Local Activity guidance](https://docs.temporal.io/local-activity) and [design notes](https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/local-activities) describe execution inside Workflow Tasks, result markers, and responsiveness constraints. Local Activities do not by themselves establish that a Workflow can host a responsive realtime race. This is an architectural hypothesis to test after model driving viability, not a settled production design.

## Implementation readiness

The user confirmed shared understanding of the experiment specification on October 18, 2026, including 60 Hz physics, 15 control choices, and a trial timeout of three times the scripted reference duration. Planning for the first PoC is complete. The next step is the offline physics and scripted-driver reference, followed by model trials when API access is available.

The local implementation and initial screens are complete. API access has been supplied and measurements are recorded under `artifacts/`. The no-rescue screen was stopped when the user requested the rescue experiment; its completed and interrupted recordings are preserved separately. The rescue timeout is an explicit game rule, not an unrecorded driving controller. The rescued raw-telemetry screen did not yield a three-lap completion; the user requested [clearer track telemetry](experiments/0002-track-telemetry.md) before further trials.

OpenRouter credentials are stored locally in the ignored `.env`. Exact provider slugs, route availability, and prices were recorded before paid runs. Clef Flash remains an optional follow-up to the three requested models.

## Later product scope

The broader concept remains autonomous three-lap racing with kart collisions, several power-ups, live spectators, public matchmaking, and service-operated bots. GitHub OAuth supplies racer identities; organization-based teams may follow. Race size remains undecided between six and eight racers.

Leaderboards should distinguish racer identity, model, and agent client or harness. Public self-reported entries and controlled model comparisons will need different evidence standards before they can support claims about the best model.

Browser spectator links, MCP Apps, and client-specific integrations need a separate compatibility investigation. A low-poly 3D presentation is a possible later evolution.

Production is intended for GCP and Temporal Serverless Workers. Hosting, service boundaries, multiplayer recovery, authentication, and capacity planning follow the local viability evidence.

"""Deterministic, unassisted solo kart simulation (metres, seconds, radians).

World coordinates are right handed: positive heading and steering turn left.
Lookahead coordinates are relative to the kart: x ahead, y left. Physics never
consults the reference driver. Its output is only used by an explicit caller.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from bisect import bisect_right
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from itertools import pairwise

DT = 1 / 60
VERSION = "solo-v2-rescue"

_STEERING = (("hard_right", -1.0), ("right", -0.5), ("straight", 0.0),
             ("left", 0.5), ("hard_left", 1.0))
_PEDALS = (("accelerate", 1.0, 0.0), ("coast", 0.0, 0.0), ("brake", 0.0, 1.0))
ACTIONS = {
    f"{name}_{pedal}": {"steer": steer, "throttle": throttle, "brake": brake,
                          "description": f"Steer {steer:+g}; {pedal}."}
    for name, steer in _STEERING
    for pedal, throttle, brake in _PEDALS
}


def wrap(angle: float) -> float:
    return (angle + math.pi) % (2 * math.pi) - math.pi


def clamp(value: float, lower: float, upper: float) -> float:
    return max(lower, min(upper, value))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Handling:
    max_speed: float = 24.0
    acceleration: float = 12.0
    braking: float = 24.0
    max_steering_angle: float = 0.32
    wheelbase: float = 1.8
    steering_response: float = 0.12
    yaw_response: float = 0.10
    lateral_grip: float = 13.0
    rolling_drag: float = 0.35
    aerodynamic_drag: float = 0.006
    grass_acceleration: float = 4.0
    grass_drag: float = 1.1
    grass_grip: float = 8.0


class Track:
    """Closed winding centreline, evenly sampled for geometry and gate checks."""

    width = 9.0

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        anchors = [(0, -25), (30, -25), (45, -10), (42, 8), (28, 17),
                   (30, 32), (8, 40), (-25, 30), (-40, 10), (-30, -18)]
        dense: list[tuple[float, float]] = []
        for i in range(len(anchors)):
            p0, p1, p2, p3 = (anchors[(i + j) % len(anchors)] for j in (-1, 0, 1, 2))
            for j in range(100):
                t = j / 100
                dense.append(tuple(0.5 * (2 * p1[k] + (-p0[k] + p2[k]) * t
                             + (2*p0[k] - 5*p1[k] + 4*p2[k] - p3[k]) * t*t
                             + (-p0[k] + 3*p1[k] - 3*p2[k] + p3[k]) * t*t*t)
                                   for k in (0, 1)))
        dense.append(dense[0])
        lengths = [0.0]
        for a, b in pairwise(dense):
            lengths.append(lengths[-1] + math.dist(a, b))
        count = 256
        self.points = []
        for i in range(count):
            s = lengths[-1] * i / count
            j = min(bisect_right(lengths, s) - 1, len(dense) - 2)
            t = (s - lengths[j]) / (lengths[j + 1] - lengths[j])
            self.points.append(tuple(a + (b-a)*t for a, b in zip(dense[j], dense[j+1])))
        self.lengths = [0.0]
        self.segments = []
        for a, b in zip(self.points, self.points[1:] + self.points[:1]):
            dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
            length = math.hypot(dx, dy)
            self.segments.append((a[0], a[1], dx, dy, length, dx/length, dy/length))
            self.lengths.append(self.lengths[-1] + length)
        self.length = self.lengths[-1]
        self.headings = []
        for i in range(count):
            a, b = self.points[(i-1) % count], self.points[(i+1) % count]
            self.headings.append(math.atan2(b[1]-a[1], b[0]-a[0]))
        self.curvatures = [wrap(self.headings[(i+1) % count] - self.headings[(i-1) % count])
                           / (self.length/count*2) for i in range(count)]
        self.checkpoints = [self.at(self.length * i / 40) for i in range(40)]

    def at(self, distance: float) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
        distance %= self.length
        i = min(bisect_right(self.lengths, distance) - 1, len(self.points) - 1)
        x, y, dx, dy, length, _, _ = self.segments[i]
        t = (distance - self.lengths[i]) / length
        j = (i+1) % len(self.points)
        heading = self.headings[i] + wrap(self.headings[j]-self.headings[i]) * t
        curvature = self.curvatures[i] + (self.curvatures[j]-self.curvatures[i]) * t
        return x+dx*t, y+dy*t, heading, curvature

    def project(self, x: float, y: float) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
        best = math.inf
        nearest_s = offset = 0.0
        for i, (ax, ay, dx, dy, length, tx, ty) in enumerate(self.segments):
            t = clamp(((x-ax)*dx + (y-ay)*dy) / (length*length), 0.0, 1.0)
            ex, ey = x - ax - dx*t, y - ay - dy*t
            squared = ex*ex + ey*ey
            if squared < best:
                best = squared
                nearest_s = self.lengths[i] + length*t
                offset = math.copysign(math.sqrt(squared), tx*ey - ty*ex)
        return nearest_s % self.length, offset, math.sqrt(best)

    def as_dict(self) -> dict:
        return {"points": [[round(x, 5), round(y, 5)] for x, y in self.points],
                "width": self.width, "length": self.length,
                "checkpoints": [{"x": x, "y": y, "heading": heading}
                                for x, y, heading, _ in self.checkpoints]}


class Simulation:
    def __init__(self, seed: int = 0, laps: int = 3,
                 reset_after_s: float | None = 3.0) -> None:
        if laps < 1:
            raise ValueError("laps must be positive")
        if reset_after_s is not None and (
            isinstance(reset_after_s, bool) or not math.isfinite(reset_after_s) or reset_after_s <= 0
        ):
            raise ValueError("reset_after_s must be positive and finite, or None")
        self.seed, self.laps = seed, laps
        self.reset_after_s = reset_after_s
        self.track, self.handling = Track(), Handling()
        rng = random.Random(seed)
        x, y, heading, _ = self.track.at(0)
        offset = rng.uniform(-0.35, 0.35)
        self.x, self.y = x - math.sin(heading)*offset, y + math.cos(heading)*offset
        self.heading = heading + rng.uniform(-0.025, 0.025)
        self.vx = self.vy = self.steering = self.yaw_rate = 0.0
        self.tick, self.elapsed = 0, 0.0
        self.finished = False
        self.action_id = "straight_coast"
        self.next_checkpoint = 1
        self.checkpoints_passed = self.laps_completed = 0
        self.lap_times: list[float] = []
        self.offroad_time = self.distance_travelled = 0.0
        self.max_speed_seen = 0.0
        self.s, self.offset, _ = self.track.project(self.x, self.y)
        self.departure_s = self.s
        self.offroad_elapsed = 0.0
        self.last_reset_tick: int | None = None
        self.reset_events: list[dict] = []

    @property
    def speed(self) -> float:
        return math.hypot(self.vx, self.vy)

    def set_control(self, action_id: str) -> None:
        if action_id not in ACTIONS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown action: {action_id}")
        self.action_id = action_id

    def _check_progress(self, old_x: float, old_y: float) -> None:
        """Cross the next finite gate forward, and only on its road surface."""
        gx, gy, heading, _ = self.track.checkpoints[self.next_checkpoint]
        tx, ty = math.cos(heading), math.sin(heading)
        before = (old_x-gx)*tx + (old_y-gy)*ty
        after = (self.x-gx)*tx + (self.y-gy)*ty
        if not (before <= 0 < after):
            return
        fraction = -before / (after-before)
        cross_x = old_x + (self.x-old_x)*fraction
        cross_y = old_y + (self.y-old_y)*fraction
        lateral = -(cross_x-gx)*ty + (cross_y-gy)*tx
        if abs(lateral) > self.track.width/2:
            return
        self.checkpoints_passed += 1
        self.next_checkpoint = (self.next_checkpoint+1) % len(self.track.checkpoints)
        if self.checkpoints_passed % len(self.track.checkpoints) == 0:
            self.laps_completed += 1
            self.lap_times.append(self.elapsed - sum(self.lap_times))
            self.finished = self.laps_completed == self.laps

    def step(self, dt: float = DT) -> None:
        if dt <= 0 or dt > DT*1.000001:
            raise ValueError("physics step must be positive and no larger than DT")
        if self.finished:
            return
        old_x, old_y, old_s = self.x, self.y, self.s
        h, action = self.handling, ACTIONS[self.action_id]
        onroad = abs(self.offset) <= self.track.width/2
        if not onroad:
            self.offroad_time += dt
            self.offroad_elapsed += dt
        else:
            self.offroad_elapsed = 0.0
        self.steering += (action["steer"]*h.max_steering_angle-self.steering) * (1-math.exp(-dt/h.steering_response))
        speed = self.speed
        forward_speed = max(0.0, self.vx*math.cos(self.heading) + self.vy*math.sin(self.heading))
        grip = h.lateral_grip if onroad else h.grass_grip
        desired_yaw = forward_speed/h.wheelbase * math.tan(self.steering)
        max_yaw = grip/max(speed, 2.0)
        desired_yaw = clamp(desired_yaw, -max_yaw, max_yaw)
        self.yaw_rate += (desired_yaw-self.yaw_rate) * (1-math.exp(-dt/h.yaw_response))
        self.heading = wrap(self.heading + self.yaw_rate*dt)
        fx, fy = math.cos(self.heading), math.sin(self.heading)
        lateral = -self.vx*fy + self.vy*fx
        lateral_change = clamp(-lateral, -grip*dt, grip*dt)
        self.vx -= fy*lateral_change
        self.vy += fx*lateral_change
        speed = self.speed
        drag = h.rolling_drag + h.aerodynamic_drag*speed*speed
        if not onroad:
            drag += h.grass_drag*speed
        acceleration = (h.acceleration if onroad else h.grass_acceleration)*action["throttle"]
        acceleration -= h.braking*action["brake"] + drag
        if acceleration < 0:
            reduction = max(0.0, speed+acceleration*dt)/speed if speed else 0.0

    preview = runtime.state()
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    stopping = asyncio.Event()
    outbox = _Outbox(connection, session_id)
    writer = threading.Thread(target=outbox.run, name="kart-ipc-writer", daemon=True)
    writer.start()
    tasks: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

    async def request(message: dict) -> None:
        if message.get("session_id") != session_id:
            return
        identity, method = message["id"], message["method"]
        try:
            arguments = message.get("arguments", {})
            if method == "start":
                value = runtime.start(**arguments)
            elif method == "observe":
                value = runtime.observe(**arguments)
            elif method == "drive":
                value = await runtime.drive(**arguments)
            elif method == "finish":
                value = runtime.finish(**arguments)
            elif method == "result":
                if runtime.current is not None and runtime.current.status == "running":
                    raise ValueError("Stop the race before transferring its full recording")
                value = runtime.result()
            elif method == "shutdown":
                await runtime.close()
                value = {"closed": True}
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"Unknown worker method: {method}")
            reply = {"type": "reply", "id": identity, "ok": True, "value": value}
            if method in {"start", "finish", "result"}:
                reply.update(state=runtime.state(), captured_ns=time.monotonic_ns())
            if method in {"finish", "result"}:
                reply["terminal_observation"] = runtime.observe()
            outbox.reply(reply)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 — propagate worker errors to their RPC caller.
            outbox.reply({"type": "reply", "id": identity, "ok": False,
                          "error_type": type(exc).__name__, "error": str(exc)})
        finally:
            if method == "shutdown":
                stopping.set()

    def dispatch(message: dict) -> None:
        task = asyncio.create_task(request(message))
        tasks.add(task)
        task.add_done_callback(tasks.discard)

    def read() -> None:
        try:
            while True:
                message = connection.recv()
                loop.call_soon_threadsafe(dispatch, message)
        except (OSError, EOFError, RuntimeError):
            try:
                loop.call_soon_threadsafe(stopping.set)
            except RuntimeError:
                pass

    reader = threading.Thread(target=read, name="kart-ipc-reader", daemon=True)
    reader.start()
    main = sys.modules.get("__main__")
    entrypoint = getattr(getattr(main, "__spec__", None), "name", None)
    outbox.reply({"type": "ready", "pid": os.getpid(), "ready_ns": time.monotonic_ns(), "state": preview,
                  "entrypoint": entrypoint,
                  "clock_mode": runtime.runtime_info()["clock_mode"],

def read_state(url: str) -> dict:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url.rstrip("/")+"/api/state", timeout=3) as response:
        return json.load(response)


class SpectatorPoller:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        self.url = url
        self.stop = threading.Event()
        self.latest: dict = {}
        self.count = self.errors = 0
        self.max_roundtrip_ms = 0.0
        self.thread = threading.Thread(target=self.run, name="validation-spectator", daemon=True)

    def run(self) -> None:
        while not self.stop.is_set():
            started = time.monotonic_ns()
            try:
                self.latest = read_state(self.url)
                self.count += 1
            except (OSError, ValueError):
                self.errors += 1
            self.max_roundtrip_ms = max(self.max_roundtrip_ms, (time.monotonic_ns()-started)/1e6)
            self.stop.wait(.05)

    def close(self) -> None:
        self.stop.set()
        self.thread.join(timeout=4)


def pause_parent(state: dict, expected_pid: int, duration: float) -> dict:
    info = state.get("runtime_info", {})
    if (info.get("backend") != "process" or info.get("process_pid") != expected_pid
            or expected_pid <= 1 or expected_pid == os.getpid()):
        raise ValueError("Refusing to signal a process that is not the verified local HTTP parent")
    started_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
    try:
        os.kill(expected_pid, signal.SIGSTOP)
        time.sleep(duration)
    finally:
        # Always resume, including on an interrupted controller sleep. SIGSTOP
        # targets the positive parent PID only, never the worker/process group.
        os.kill(expected_pid, signal.SIGCONT)
    ended_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
    return {"parent_pid": expected_pid, "race_id": state["race_id"], "started_ns": started_ns,
            "ended_ns": ended_ns, "requested_duration_s": duration,
            "actual_duration_s": (ended_ns-started_ns)/1e9,
            "last_polled_tick": state["observation"]["tick"],
            "last_polled_race_s": state["observation"]["time"], "signals": ["SIGSTOP", "SIGCONT"]}

            self.current.diagnostics.span(name, started_ns, started_cpu_ns)

    def _state(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        race = self.current
        if race is None:
            if self._preview is None:
                self._preview = Simulation(seed=0, laps=3)
            preview = self._preview
            return {"status": "idle", "track": preview.track.as_dict(), "actions": ACTIONS, "config": preview.config()}
        now = time.monotonic_ns()
        # This read does not count as a model observation.
        observation = {**race.sim.observation(), "race_id": race.race_id, "status": race.status}
        return {
            "status": race.status, "race_id": race.race_id, "label": race.label,
            "reason": race.reason, "seed": race.seed, "deadline": race.deadline,
            "observation": observation, "track": race.sim.track.as_dict(), "actions": ACTIONS,
            "timing": self._timing(race), "command_count": len(race.commands),
            "waiting_for_reply": race.status == "running" and race.pending is None,
            "observation_age_ms": None if race.last_observed_ns is None else (now - race.last_observed_ns) / 1e6,
            "trail": [[s["kart"]["x"], s["kart"]["y"]] for s in race.samples[-600::3]
                      if s["tick"] >= (race.sim.last_reset_tick or 0)],
        }

    async def close(self) -> None:
        if self.current is not None and self.current.status == "running":
            self.finish(reason="server_shutdown")
        task = self.current.task if self.current is not None else None
"""Free real-MCP controls with HTTP polling and one declared parent-process pause.

Run against this project's local process-backend development server. This never
loads model credentials or runs a model command. All evidence goes to a fresh
artifact directory, including failed controls.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import os
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlparse


def read_state(url: str) -> dict:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url.rstrip("/")+"/api/state", timeout=3) as response:
        return json.load(response)


class SpectatorPoller:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        self.url = url
        self.stop = threading.Event()
        self.latest: dict = {}
        self.count = self.errors = 0
        self.max_roundtrip_ms = 0.0
        self.thread = threading.Thread(target=self.run, name="validation-spectator", daemon=True)

    def run(self) -> None:
        while not self.stop.is_set():
            started = time.monotonic_ns()
            try:
                self.latest = read_state(self.url)
                self.count += 1
            except (OSError, ValueError):
                self.errors += 1
            self.max_roundtrip_ms = max(self.max_roundtrip_ms, (time.monotonic_ns()-started)/1e6)
            self.stop.wait(.05)

    def close(self) -> None:
        self.stop.set()
        self.thread.join(timeout=4)


def pause_parent(state: dict, expected_pid: int, duration: float) -> dict:
    info = state.get("runtime_info", {})
    if (info.get("backend") != "process" or info.get("process_pid") != expected_pid
            or expected_pid <= 1 or expected_pid == os.getpid()):
        raise ValueError("Refusing to signal a process that is not the verified local HTTP parent")
    started_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
    try:
        os.kill(expected_pid, signal.SIGSTOP)
        time.sleep(duration)
    finally:
        # Always resume, including on an interrupted controller sleep. SIGSTOP
        # targets the positive parent PID only, never the worker/process group.
        os.kill(expected_pid, signal.SIGCONT)
    ended_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
    return {"parent_pid": expected_pid, "race_id": state["race_id"], "started_ns": started_ns,
            "ended_ns": ended_ns, "requested_duration_s": duration,
            "actual_duration_s": (ended_ns-started_ns)/1e9,
            "last_polled_tick": state["observation"]["tick"],
            "last_polled_race_s": state["observation"]["time"], "signals": ["SIGSTOP", "SIGCONT"]}


def run(args) -> dict:
    if urlparse(args.url).hostname not in {"127.0.0.1", "localhost", "::1"}:
        raise ValueError("Clock validation only signals a local development server")
    initial = read_state(args.url)
    info = initial.get("runtime_info", {})
    if (info.get("backend") != "process" or info.get("process_pid") != args.parent_pid
            or info.get("clock_mode") != args.clock_mode):
        raise ValueError("Server must report the expected process backend, clock mode and parent PID")
    output = Path(args.output)
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    poller = SpectatorPoller(args.url)
    poller.thread.start()
    rows, pause = [], None
    report = {"script_sha256": hashlib.sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
              "runtime_info": info, "expected_clock_mode": args.clock_mode,
              "reference": args.reference, "required_consecutive_controls": 3,
              "pause_run": 2, "pause_at_s": args.pause_at, "pause_duration_s": args.pause_for,
              "validity_limits_ms": {"max_lateness": 100, "p95_lateness": 25, "absolute_drift": 100},
              "model_requests": 0, "controls": rows, "passes": False}
    try:
        for index in range(1, 4):
            directory = output/f"run-{index:02d}"
            count_before = poller.count
            command = [sys.executable, "-m", "mcpkart.bench", "live-reference", "--url",
                       args.url.rstrip("/")+"/mcp", "--reference", args.reference, "--output", str(directory)]
            with (output/f"run-{index:02d}.log").open("w") as log:
                process = subprocess.Popen(command, stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
                try:
                    while process.poll() is None:
                        state = poller.latest
                        if (index == 2 and pause is None and state.get("status") == "running"
                                and state.get("observation", {}).get("time", 0) >= args.pause_at):
                            # Revalidate identity via a fresh response immediately
                            # before signaling, rather than trust an old PID.
                            pause = pause_parent(read_state(args.url), args.parent_pid, args.pause_for)
                        time.sleep(.02)
                    if process.returncode:
                        raise RuntimeError(f"Control {index} failed; see {log.name}")
                finally:
                    if process.poll() is None:
                        process.terminate()
                        try:
                            process.wait(timeout=5)
                        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                            process.kill()
                            process.wait()
            path = directory/"scripted-live.json"
            trial = json.loads(path.read_text())
            race, metrics = trial["race"], trial["metrics"]
            row = {"trial": str(path), "fingerprint": trial["fingerprint"],
                   "runtime_info": trial["runtime_info"], "metrics": metrics,
                   "checkpoints_passed": race["summary"]["checkpoints_passed"],
                   "spectator_polls": poller.count-count_before}
            row["passes"] = bool(metrics["finished"] and metrics["realtime_valid"]
                                 and row["checkpoints_passed"] == 120 and row["spectator_polls"] > 0)
            if index == 2:
                if pause is None or pause["race_id"] != race["race_id"]:
                    raise RuntimeError("The declared parent-pause injection did not occur in control 2")
                samples = [sample for sample in race["samples"]
                           if pause["started_ns"] <= sample["wall_ns"] <= pause["ended_ns"]]
                pause["physics_samples_during_parent_pause"] = len(samples)
                pause["maximum_child_lateness_during_parent_pause_ms"] = max(
                    (sample["lateness_ms"] for sample in samples), default=None)
                row["passes"] = row["passes"] and len(samples) >= 12
                row["parent_pause"] = pause
            rows.append(row)
            print(json.dumps({"run": index, "passes": row["passes"], "elapsed": metrics["elapsed"],
                              "max_lateness_ms": metrics["timing"]["max_lateness_ms"]}), flush=True)
            if not row["passes"]:
                # Preserve failure and stop. Do not search repeatedly for three
                # lucky successes while hiding intervening invalid controls.
                break
        report["passes"] = len(rows) == 3 and all(row["passes"] for row in rows)
        report["source_unchanged"] = len({row["fingerprint"] for row in rows}) <= 1
        report["passes"] = report["passes"] and report["source_unchanged"]
        return report
"}}

Yes—a bounded Rust worker spike is reasonable. The code already gives it a clean architectural boundary.

- Keep Python’s FastMCP/HTTP server, benchmark driver, OpenRouter client, spectator UI, and future Temporal orchestration.
- Replace only the fresh race-worker subprocess: simulation state, 60 Hz clock, queued input application, observations, rescue/progress rules, recording, and timing diagnostics.
- Use a dedicated Rust simulation thread with absolute tick deadlines. Feed it bounded commands; publish immutable snapshots through a bounded latest-value channel. Keep serialization, pipe writes, percentile calculations, and full recording export outside the tick thread.
- Start with ordinary IPC such as framed JSON. A Python extension would leave interpreter/GIL interactions in the comparison and creates a less useful deployment boundary.

The important current coupling: [`process_runtime.py:144`](/Users/atbaker/Projects/atbaker/mcpkart/src/mcpkart/process_runtime.py:144) builds spectator state every 50 ms on the **same child asyncio loop as physics**. [`runtime.py:442`](/Users/atbaker/Projects/atbaker/mcpkart/src/mcpkart/runtime.py:442) reconstructs telemetry, static track data, trail, and timing statistics. IPC writing has its own thread, but Python serialization still shares that child’s GIL. This offers a plausible Rust benefit, not a demonstrated cause.

What the evidence supports:

- Linux physics-step maximum was **0.81 ms**, well below a **16.67 ms** tick budget: insufficient numerical throughput is not established.
- Linux’s worst delay overlaps a **102 ms CPU-accounted state-publication span**. Process CPU covers every worker thread; it does not identify `_state` or the GIL as the cause.
- Several earlier macOS gaps had little child CPU and also affected independent heartbeat processes. Rust cannot guarantee removal of shared-host scheduling pauses.
- One valid Python Jev screen already achieved timing limits while failing driving. Rust may unblock measurement; it will not itself repair model anticipation or gate recovery.

Fair comparison pitfalls:

1. Preserve track coordinates, initial pose, physics constants, 15 controls, 60 Hz, rescue semantics, command sequencing, stale-observation checks, and 100/25/100 ms limits.
2. Export initial conditions and geometry from Python fixtures rather than attempting to reproduce Python’s RNG/track generation immediately.
3. Expect small cross-language floating-point/libm differences. Use documented tolerances for pose replay, exact logical checks for controls, gates, resets, elapsed ticks, and physics configuration; do not silently recalibrate handling.
4. Run release builds with initialization before the epoch and identical MCP/spectator load. Preserve failures and the existing three-control/long-duration gate.
5. A Rust implementation with a dedicated tick thread changes architecture as well as language. Call it a practical engine comparison, not proof that Python alone caused stalls.
6. Do not add collisions, power-ups, a game engine framework, or production infrastructure before the timing comparison. That would obscure the question and expand the port.

The spike should first reproduce the current solo race behind the existing Python-facing API, pass deterministic fixtures and timing controls, then resume the already declared Jev navigation screen.

**Yes—I think a bounded Rust race-engine trial is worthwhile now.** Keeping Python and FastMCP around it makes sense.

The evidence points toward timing predictability rather than physics throughput: our slowest Linux physics step was **0.81 ms**, comfortably within a **16.67 ms** tick budget. The troublesome delay overlapped **102 ms of state-publication work**. That makes the whole clock-owning runtime the useful boundary to test.

I’d split responsibilities this way:

- **Rust:** simulation state, 60 Hz clock, control application, checkpoints, rescues, and compact snapshots. A dedicated simulation thread would hand snapshots to other threads for encoding and transport.
- **Python:** FastMCP, model requests, benchmark tooling, spectator server, and eventual Temporal orchestration.

Rust gives us more control over memory allocation and concurrent work inside the engine. It still depends on OS scheduling; even Rust’s [sleep documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.sleep.html) explicitly allows delayed wakeups. The shared Mac host therefore remains a possible source of stalls.

For the experiment, I’d reproduce the **current solo game**, verify it against saved Python trajectories, and run the same scripted controls and timing limits through FastMCP. """Process-isolated physics with lossless RPC and coalesced spectator snapshots.

The child imports no web or MCP framework. Its asyncio loop never writes a
pipe: a separate writer owns serialization/backpressure, and only compact state
is published while the physics clock runs. Full recordings leave after stop.

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import multiprocessing as mp
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
import uuid
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

from .runtime import ASYNCIO_CLOCK_MODE, NATIVE_CLOCK_MODE, RaceRuntime
from .sim import ACTIONS, DT, Simulation


class _Outbox:
    def __init__(self, connection, session_id: str) -> None:
        self.connection, self.session_id = connection, session_id
        self.condition = threading.Condition()
        self.replies: deque[dict] = deque()
        self.latest: dict | None = None
        self.closed = False
        self.failed = threading.Event()

    def reply(self, value: dict) -> None:
        with self.condition:
            if len(self.replies) >= 128:
                self.failed.set()
                raise RuntimeError("Worker RPC reply queue exhausted")
            self.replies.append({**value, "session_id": self.session_id})
            self.condition.notify()

    def publish(self, state: dict) -> None:
        with self.condition:
            self.latest = {"type": "state", "session_id": self.session_id,
                           "captured_ns": time.monotonic_ns(), "state": state}
            self.condition.notify()

    def run(self) -> None:
        try:
            while True:
                with self.condition:
                    self.condition.wait_for(lambda: self.replies or self.latest is not None or self.closed)
                    if self.replies:
                        value = self.replies.popleft()
                    elif self.latest is not None:
                        value, self.latest = self.latest, None
                    else:
                        return
                # Never hold the publication lock across serialization/write.
                self.connection.send(value)
        except (OSError, EOFError):
            self.failed.set()

    def close(self) -> None:
        with self.condition:
            self.closed = True
            self.condition.notify()


async def _worker_loop(connection, session_id: str, watchdog: bool, native_sleeper: bool) -> None:
    runtime = RaceRuntime(watchdog=watchdog, native_sleeper=native_sleeper)
    # Initialize the immutable track/handling and interpreter paths before any
    # race epoch. HTTP/MCP/application metadata is absent from this process.
    preview = runtime.state()
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    stopping = asyncio.Event()
    outbox = _Outbox(connection, session_id)
    writer = threading.Thread(target=outbox.run, name="kart-ipc-writer", daemon=True)
    writer.start()
    tasks: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

    async def request(message: dict) -> None:
        if message.get("session_id") != session_id:
            return
        identity, method = message["id"], message["method"]
        try:
            arguments = message.get("arguments", {})
            if method == "start":
                value = runtime.start(**arguments)
            elif method == "observe":
                value = runtime.observe(**arguments)
            elif method == "drive":
                value = await runtime.drive(**arguments)
            elif method == "finish":
                value = runtime.finish(**arguments)
            elif method == "result":
                if runtime.current is not None and runtime.current.status == "running":
                    raise ValueError("Stop the race before transferring its full recording")
                value = runtime.result()
            elif method == "shutdown":
                await runtime.close()
                value = {"closed": True}
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"Unknown worker method: {method}")

                reply.update(state=runtime.state(), captured_ns=time.monotonic_ns())

                loop.call_soon_threadsafe(dispatch, message)

                loop.call_soon_threadsafe(stopping.set)
            except RuntimeError:
                pass

    reader.start()

    entrypoint = getattr(getattr(main, "__spec__", None), "name", None)
    outbox.reply({"type": "ready", "pid": os.getpid(), "ready_ns": time.monotonic_ns(), "state": preview,
                  "entrypoint": entrypoint,
                  "clock_mode": runtime.runtime_info()["clock_mode"],
                  "web_modules_loaded": [name for name in ("fastmcp", "starlette", "uvicorn") if name in sys.modules]})

        # an active clock, and the parent's shutdown path can terminate us.

    def __init__(self, fd: int, session_id: str, watchdog: bool, native_sleeper: bool) -> None:

        if native_sleeper:

        return self.process.pid if self.process is not None else None

    def start(self) -> None:
        self.process = subprocess.Popen(self.arguments, pass_fds=(self.fd,), close_fds=True)

    def is_alive(self) -> bool:
        return self.process is not None and self.process.poll() is None

    def join(self, timeout: float) -> None:
        if self.process is not None:

            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:

        if self.process is not None:

        if self.process is not None:

# Proposed Rust race-engine experiment

October 18, 2026. Status: proposed; no Rust port or timed Rust trials have run.
The user asked whether Rust is worth trying for the game engine while retaining
Python and FastMCP for the platform. The recommendation is a bounded race-worker
experiment before choosing a production implementation language.

## Evidence and hypothesis

The [Linux control](0006-linux-docker-clock.md) completed three laps, but failed
the unchanged maximum-lateness gate: 104.26 ms versus 100 ms. Its maximum
physics-step duration was only 0.81 ms, well below a 16.67 ms tick budget. A
102 ms state-publication span coincided with the worst delayed wake and
substantial process CPU. Process CPU covers all child threads; neither that
function nor the GIL is established as the cause. Earlier low-CPU macOS gaps
remain a separate clue. Linux runs in Docker's VM on the same Mac.

Inferred from current source, not checkpoint history: the isolated Python
worker still runs physics, observation construction and its 20 Hz state
publisher on one asyncio loop. IPC serialization runs on a separate Python
thread in that same process. Porting only the vehicle equations would leave
these possible sources of delay in place.

Rust offers a useful alternative implementation for the entire clock-owning
worker: compiled code, explicit memory ownership, and OS threads without
Python's GIL. Rust ownership avoids tracing garbage collection, but GC was
short in the failed Linux control, so that benefit alone is not an explanation.
Rust is not a realtime scheduling guarantee; its documented sleep behavior
permits oversleep because of OS scheduling. See the official
[ownership chapter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership.html)
and [thread sleep documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.sleep.html).

## Smallest useful boundary

Keep Python for FastMCP, the model driver, benchmark scoring, HTTP/SVG
spectating, and eventual platform orchestration. Replace the race-worker
process behind the existing runtime interface with a standalone Rust binary.
Do not introduce an embedded Python extension or a new physics library for
this comparison.

The Rust clock thread owns simulation state and absolute 60 Hz deadlines.
It applies bounded, validated commands at tick boundaries and produces compact
snapshots. Other threads encode responses and write transport messages.
Snapshot publication must be bounded and nonblocking, with older spectator
snapshots replaceable; applied-command acknowledgements remain lossless or
fail explicitly. A blocked Python parent must not block the clock thread.
Preallocate trial recording capacity and export it after stop. Keep variable
work, formatting, transport writes, and cumulative percentile calculations
off the tick thread; changing language does not make that work harmless.

Preserve the current handling equations, track, 15 controls, checkpoint rules,
three-second rescue at zero speed, stale-command rejection, and observation
semantics. Supply exact track geometry and initial state from Python fixtures
so RNG or spline implementations cannot silently change the course. Keep
the existing telemetry candidate and model instructions fixed.

## Evaluation order

1. Port deterministic simulation and replay saved applied inputs at their
   recorded ticks. Declare numerical tolerances before comparison; require
   exact discrete outcomes (controls, gates, laps, rescue ticks). Preserve the
   Python reference. Investigate divergent boundary events before live trials;
   do not silently recalibrate handling to make a run pass.
2. Run a headless Rust clock with stationary state, then the scripted driver
   through Python/FastMCP with spectator polling. Record release-build and
   dependency identity, per-thread CPU, tick lateness, action age, snapshots
   and backpressure. Include a deliberately paused Python parent.
3. Use the existing gate: three consecutive valid scripted three-lap controls,
   then the 170.1 s neutral-input check. Keep maximum lateness <=100 ms,
   p95 <=25 ms, and absolute final drift <=100 ms; stop and preserve the first
   failed control. Compare in the same Docker VM/resources first, with native
   macOS as a separately labelled check. Finish builds and analysis before
   timed runs.
4. Only after the free gate passes, resume one Jev screen with the existing
   reference, telemetry, route and shared $10 budget. Free Rust experiments
   require no API credentials.

A pass establishes that this Rust worker architecture can support the current
local workload. It does not prove that Python is inherently too slow: language,
threading and publication design changed together. A failure keeps host/VM
scheduling and transport design in scope. Multiplayer collisions, power-ups,
framework adoption and production hosting follow the solo driving milestone.

    def __init__(self, fd: int, session_id: str, watchdog: bool, native_sleeper: bool) -> None:
        self.arguments = [sys.executable, "-m", "mcpkart.physics_worker", "--worker-fd", str(fd), "--session", session_id]
        if watchdog:
            self.arguments.append("--watchdog")
        if native_sleeper:
            self.arguments.append("--native-sleeper")
        self.fd = fd
        self.process: subprocess.Popen | None = None

    @property
    def pid(self) -> int | None:
        return self.process.pid if self.process is not None else None

    def start(self) -> None:
        self.process = subprocess.Popen(self.arguments, pass_fds=(self.fd,), close_fds=True)

    def is_alive(self) -> bool:
        return self.process is not None and self.process.poll() is None

    def join(self, timeout: float) -> None:
        if self.process is not None:
            try:
                self.process.wait(timeout=timeout)
            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                pass

    def terminate(self) -> None:
        if self.process is not None:
            self.process.terminate()

    def kill(self) -> None:
        if self.process is not None:
            self.process.kill()

The [Linux control](0006-linux-docker-clock.md) completed three laps, but failed
the unchanged maximum-lateness gate: 104.26 ms versus 100 ms. Its maximum
physics-step duration was only 0.81 ms, well below a 16.67 ms tick budget. A

substantial process CPU. Process CPU covers all child threads; neither that
function nor the GIL is established as the cause. Earlier low-CPU macOS gaps
remain a separate clue. Linux runs in Docker's VM on the same Mac.

Inferred from current source, not checkpoint history: the isolated Python
worker still runs physics, observation construction and its 20 Hz state
publisher on one asyncio loop. IPC serialization runs on a separate Python
thread in that same process. Porting only the vehicle equations would leave
these possible sources of delay in place.

Rust offers a useful alternative implementation for the entire clock-owning
worker: compiled code, explicit memory ownership, and OS threads without
Python's GIL. Rust ownership avoids tracing garbage collection, but GC was
short in the failed Linux control, so that benefit alone is not an explanation.
Rust is not a realtime scheduling guarantee; its documented sleep behavior
permits oversleep because of OS scheduling. See the official
[ownership chapter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership.html)
and [thread sleep documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.sleep.html).

## Smallest useful boundary

Keep Python for FastMCP, the model driver, benchmark scoring, HTTP/SVG
spectating, and eventual platform orchestration. Replace the race-worker
process behind the existing runtime interface with a standalone Rust binary.
Do not introduce an embedded Python extension or a new physics library for
this comparison.

The Rust clock thread owns simulation state and absolute 60 Hz deadlines.
It applies bounded, validated commands at tick boundaries and produces compact
snapshots. Other threads encode responses and write transport messages.
Snapshot publication must be bounded and nonblocking, with older spectator
snapshots replaceable; applied-command acknowledgements remain lossless or
fail explicitly. A blocked Python parent must not block the clock thread.
Preallocate trial recording capacity and export it after stop. Keep variable
work, formatting, transport writes, and cumulative percentile calculations
off the tick thread; changing language does not make that work harmless.

Preserve the current handling equations, track, 15 controls, checkpoint rules,
three-second rescue at zero speed, stale-command rejection, and observation
semantics. Supply exact track geometry and initial state from Python fixtures
so RNG or spline implementations cannot silently change the course. Keep
the existing telemetry candidate and model instructions fixed.

## Evaluation order

1. Port deterministic simulation and replay saved applied inputs at their
   recorded ticks. Declare numerical tolerances before comparison; require
   exact discrete outcomes (controls, gates, laps, rescue ticks). Preserve the
   Python reference. Investigate divergent boundary events before live trials;
   do not silently recalibrate handling to make a run pass.
2. Run a headless Rust clock with stationary state, then the scripted driver
   through Python/FastMCP with spectator polling. Record release-build and
   dependency identity, per-thread CPU, tick lateness, action age, snapshots

import time
from threading import Event

import pytest

from mcpkart.process_runtime import ProcessRaceRuntime
from mcpkart.runtime import ASYNCIO_CLOCK_MODE, NATIVE_CLOCK_MODE
from mcpkart.sim import Simulation


@pytest.mark.asyncio
@pytest.mark.parametrize("native_sleeper", [False, True])
async def test_child_clock_survives_parent_loop_block_and_acknowledges_real_application(native_sleeper):
    # Omitting the flag must retain the old asyncio process default.
    runtime = ProcessRaceRuntime(native_sleeper=True) if native_sleeper else ProcessRaceRuntime()
    clock_mode = NATIVE_CLOCK_MODE if native_sleeper else ASYNCIO_CLOCK_MODE
    assert runtime.runtime_info()["clock_mode"] == clock_mode
    try:
        initial = await runtime.start(deadline=3, label="Isolation control")
        assert ("--native-sleeper" in runtime._session.process.arguments) == native_sleeper
        assert runtime._session.clock_mode == clock_mode
        submitted_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
        ack = await runtime.drive(initial["race_id"], "straight_accelerate", initial["tick"], 0)
        assert ack["applied"]
        assert ack["applied_tick"] > initial["tick"]
        assert submitted_ns <= ack["queued_ns"] <= ack["applied_ns"] <= ack["observation"]["observed_ns"]
        before = await runtime.observe()
        block_started_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
        time.sleep(.25)  # noqa: ASYNC251 — deliberately block the parent, never the child.
        block_ended_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
        after = await runtime.observe()
        assert after["tick"]-before["tick"] >= 12
        assert after["time"]-before["time"] >= .2
        assert after["control"] == "straight_accelerate"
        assert after["kart"]["speed"] > before["kart"]["speed"]
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Stop the race"):
            await runtime.result()
        state = runtime.state()
        assert state["snapshot_age_ms"] >= 0
        assert "samples" not in state and "commands" not in state
        result = await runtime.finish(reason="test_finished")
        assert result["runtime_info"]["backend"] == "process"
        assert result["runtime_info"]["clock_mode"] == result["timing"]["clock_mode"] == clock_mode
        provenance = result["process_provenance"]
        assert provenance["child_pid"] != os.getpid()
        assert result["runtime_info"]["process_pid"] == os.getpid()
        assert provenance["worker_module"] == "mcpkart.physics_worker"
        assert provenance["child_web_modules_loaded"] == []
        assert provenance["child_clock_mode"] == clock_mode
        assert provenance["worker_ready_ns"] <= provenance["clock_started_ns"]
        if native_sleeper:
            assert result["timing"]["pacing"]["native_sleeper_ready_ns"] <= provenance["clock_started_ns"]
        else:
            assert result["timing"]["pacing"]["native_sleeper_ready_ns"] is None
        assert result["timing"]["pacing"]["native_sleeper_thread_alive"] is False
        assert result["commands"][0]["applied_ns"] == ack["applied_ns"]
        assert sum(block_started_ns < sample["wall_ns"] < block_ended_ns for sample in result["samples"]) >= 10
        # Validate the recorded applied-tick contract by reproducing every pose,
        # rather than merely checking that an acknowledgement carried a value.
        sim = Simulation(seed=result["seed"], laps=result["config"]["laps"],
                         reset_after_s=result["config"]["rescue"]["after_s"])
        commands = {command["applied_tick"]: command["action_id"] for command in result["commands"]}
        for sample in result["samples"]:

        assert late["applied"] is False
    finally:
        await runtime.close()

        deadline = time.monotonic()+3

    original_rpc, original_shutdown = runtime._rpc, runtime._shutdown

    async def delayed_rpc(name, arguments=None, *, session=None):
        value = await original_rpc(name, arguments, session=session)
        if name == method and asyncio.current_task() is collecting and pause_phase == "before_cache":
            paused.set()
            await release.wait()
        return value

    async def delayed_shutdown(*, session):
        if asyncio.current_task() is collecting and pause_phase == "before_cleanup":
            paused.set()
            await release.wait()
        await original_shutdown(session=session)

    monkeypatch.setattr(runtime, "_rpc", delayed_rpc)
    monkeypatch.setattr(runtime, "_shutdown", delayed_shutdown)

        if method == "result":

async def test_child_clock_survives_parent_loop_block_and_acknowledges_real_application(native_sleeper):
    # Omitting the flag must retain the old asyncio process default.
    runtime = ProcessRaceRuntime(native_sleeper=True) if native_sleeper else ProcessRaceRuntime()
    clock_mode = NATIVE_CLOCK_MODE if native_sleeper else ASYNCIO_CLOCK_MODE

        after = await runtime.observe()

        assert after["kart"]["speed"] > before["kart"]["speed"]
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Stop the race"):
            await runtime.result()
        state = runtime.state()
        assert state["snapshot_age_ms"] >= 0
        assert "samples" not in state and "commands" not in state
        result = await runtime.finish(reason="test_finished")

        assert result["runtime_info"]["clock_mode"] == result["timing"]["clock_mode"] == clock_mode
        provenance = result["process_provenance"]

        assert result["runtime_info"]["process_pid"] == os.getpid()
        assert provenance["worker_module"] == "mcpkart.physics_worker"
        assert provenance["child_web_modules_loaded"] == []
        assert provenance["child_clock_mode"] == clock_mode
        assert provenance["worker_ready_ns"] <= provenance["clock_started_ns"]
        if native_sleeper:

    source = Path(__file__).parent
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    for name in (
        "sim.py",
        "decisions.py",
        "runtime.py",
        "process_runtime.py",
        "physics_worker.py",
